items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:A9857

TITLE  OF BILL:   An act to amend the estates, powers and trusts law, in
relation to credit shelter formula bequests  after  federal  estate  tax
repeal  and  bequests of unused federal generation skipping transfer tax
exemption after repeal

PURPOSE:  This bill is designed to prevent  the  inadvertent  disinheri-
tance of a surviving spouse by virtue of the recent repeal of the Feder-
al estate tax.

Under the newly revised Internal Revenue Code, the Federal estate tax is
repealed  for  decedent's  dying in 2010, only to be restored in 2011 at
higher rates and with lower exemptions. Most estate  attorneys  expected
Congress  to  enact  a new law prior to 2010 so as to prevent the estate
tax from expiring and did not anticipate  that  temporary  repeal  would
occur.  There  is  still  a  possibility  that Congress may reinstate an
estate tax for 2010 retroactively.

Many wills, trusts and beneficiary forms prepared  prior  to  2010  were
based  on formula dispositions in the case of married testators. The aim
was typically to leave as much as possible on- the first spouse's  death
to  a trust or to individuals other than the surviving spouse (typically
issue of the decedent) without causing estate tax on the first  spouse's
death.  This  was  commonly  referred  hi as a "credit shelter bequest",
since the amount involved ($3.5 million for a decedent  dying  in  2009)
would  be  sheltered  from  estate  tax on the first death by a "unified
credit" allowed under the Internal  Revenue  Code.  The  credit  shelter
bequest is not subject to estate tax.on the surviving spouse's death.

The  credit  shelter  bequest is usually phrased in terms of the maximum
amount that can pass free of Federal estate tax on the first  death,  or
in  terms  of  like effect. The same results were obtained with formulas
leaving a spouse  outright  or  in  a  form  qualifying  for  a  marital
deduction  against  the Federal estate tax, the minimum amount necessary
to avoid imposition of an estate tax on the first spouse's  death.  With
repeal  of the estate tax, these formula clauses could be interpreted to
leave the entire estate in a credit shelter disposition and  nothing  to
the spouse or in a form qualifying for a marital deduction. This conclu-
sion  is  reached since the entire estate and not just the part formerly
sheltered by statutory credits can  now  pass  under  a  credit  shelter
disposition without there being any estate tax.

The  Federal  generation  skipping  transfer  tax  is  also  temporarily
repealed for transfers in 2010. Many wills and testamentary  instruments
also  left  to grandchildren (or to trusts that would eventually pass to
grandchildren) maximum amounts allowable without imposition of a Federal
generation skipping transfer tax. With repeal, this amount is now unlim-
ited, and may pass to grandchildren to the detriment of  the  decedent's
children.

The purposes of the bill, accordingly, are:

1.  To  preserve the form in which most testators expected their estates
to be divided prior to the unexpected repeal of the Federal estate tax;

2.  To  assure that a surviving spouse will not be disinherited and left
to exercise a right of election under Article 5 of the  Estates,  Powers
and Trusts Law;

3. To shelter assets in a credit shelter disposition for the time estate
tax may be reinstated;

4.  To  prevent unwarranted amounts from passing to grandchildren to the
detriment of children.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:  The bill amends the Estates, Powers  and  Trusts
Law  to  provide  that  a  formula  in a will, trust or beneficiary form
executed or created prior to January  1,  2010  providing,  in  sum  and
substance,  for  a bequest of the maximum amount of property that can be
sheltered from Federal estate tax by reason of credits against such tax,
shall be construed under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 as in  effect
for  decedents dying on December 31, 2009, in the case of a decedent who
is survived by a spouse, and who dies at a time when the Federal  estate
tax  is repealed. The Federal estate tax is not deemed repealed if it is
legally reinstated retroactively to the time of the decedent's death.

Similarly, if a will,  trust  or  beneficiary  designation  executed  or
created  prior to January 1, 2010 contains a bequest which is in sum and
substance equal to the decedent's  unused  exemption  from  the  federal
generation  skipping  transfer tax, then such bequest shall be construed
under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 in effect on December 31,  2009,
in  the case of a decedent who dies when the federal generation skipping
transfer tax is not_ in effect. Again, the federal  generation  skipping
transfer  tax  is  considered  to  be  in  effect  if legally reinstated
retroactively to the date of decedent's death.

EXISTING LAW:  Existing Law following repeal of the Federal  estate  tax
and  generation skipping transfer tax is unclear, It is conceivable that
all of a decedent's property may be held by a  court  to  pass  under  a
credit shelter disposition to the detriment of a surviving spouse.

It  is also possible that a decedent's children may be deprived of prop-
erty all of which is held to pass under a bequest of a decedent's unused
exemption from the Federal generation skipping transfer tax.

JUSTIFICATION:  See discussion under proposed bill.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:  None

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:  Minimal

EFFECTIVE DATE:  This bill takes effect immediately.

BILL NUMBER:A9857B

TITLE  OF BILL:   An act to amend the estates, powers and trusts law, in
relation to certain formula clauses to be  construed  to  refer  to  the
federal  estate  and generation-skipping transfer tax laws applicable to
estates of decedents dying after December 31, 2009 and before January 1,
2011

now unlimited, and may pass to grandchildren to  the  detriment  of  the
decedent's children.

The purposes of the bill, accordingly, are:

2. To assure that a surviving spouse will not be disinherited  and  left

4.  To  prevent unwarranted amounts from passing to grandchildren to the

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:   The bill, which  applies  to  assets  that  are

trust, amends the Estates, Powers and  Trusts  Law  to  provide  that  a
formula  in  a will, trust or beneficiary form executed or created prior
to January 1, 2010 providing, in sum and substance, for a bequest of  an
amount  of  property  that  can  be sheltered from Federal estate tax by
reason of credits against such tax, shall be construed under the  Inter-
nal  Revenue  Code  of 1986 as in effect for decedents dying on December
31, 2009, in the case of a decedent who is survived by a spouse, and who
dies during 2010 at a time when the Federal estate tax is repealed.  The
Federal estate tax is not deemed repealed if it  is  legally  reinstated
retroactively to the time of the decedent's death. This legislation does
not apply to irrevocable trusts.

Similarly,  if  a  will,  trust  or  beneficiary designation executed or
created prior to January 1, 2010 contains a bequest  which  in  sum  and
substance  refers  to  the  decedent's unused exemption from the federal

al generation skipping transfer tax is not in effect, Again, the federal
generation skipping transfer tax is considered to be in effect if legal-
ly reinstated retroactively to the date of decedent's death.

This legislation also includes a provision exempting any will  or  trust
that  already  has  provisions  drafted by the testator determining what
should happen with formula clause provisions in the event that estate or
generation-skipping transfer tax is repealed.

Finally, this legislation provides that any affected beneficiary or  the
executor  or  trustee  may  bring  a  proceeding  within  a  year of the
decedent's date of death to determine whether the decedent intended that
that the formula clause be construed with  respect  to  the  law  as  it
existed  on  the  decedent's  date of death (rather than on December 31,
2009). In that regard, the  legislation  also  provides  that  extrinsic

and generation skipping transfer tax is unclear. It is conceivable  that
all  of  a  decedent's  property  may be held by a court to pass under a

exemption from the Federal generation skipping transfer tax.

estate and generation skipping tax, when there is a formula clause in  a
will,  the  intent  of  the testator cannot be carried out or determined
through a construction proceeding. The only remedy available is a costly
right of election proceeding that may very well be  contested  by  other
beneficiaries. This legislation will therefore avoid needless litigation
to  the benefit of beneficiaries of the decedent and the court system as
well.

fiscal  implications.  However there would be additional New York estate
tax if, in the absence of the bill, courts require the entire estate  to
pass under a formula credit shelter disposition.

EFFECTIVE  DATE:    This act shall take effect immediately, and shall be
deemed to have been in full force and effect on  and  after  January  1,
2010.
